segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: Oh, there you are, good. Sorry I'm a bit late- there was a long queue. So, have you worked out how to deal with this assignment then?

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: Not yet, we've only been here a couple of minutes ourselves.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: Can you just remind me what the task is exactly?

segments.speaker: PETE
segments.en: Well, there are two, no, three, parts to it: first, we've got to write an essay about ways of collecting data. Then . . .

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: What's the title of the essay exactly?

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: I've got it here: 'Assess the two main methods of collecting data in social science research'.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: And how much do we need to write?

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: Fifteen hundred words. That's for the essay. Then. for the second part of the assignment, we have to choose one method of data collection, and 'carry out a small-scale study, making appropriate use of the method chosen to gather data from at least five subjects'.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: And then we have to write a report on the study?

segments.speaker: PETE
segments.en: That's right. of three to four thousand words.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: Did you get as far as discussing which form of data collection we should go for - questionnaire or interview, isn't it?

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: Yeah, I think we should use a questionnaire. It'll be so much less time-consuming than organising interviews, I reckon. Once we've agreed on the wording of it, we only have to send it out and wait for the responses.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: Yes, I think it probably would be quicker. But what did that article he gave us last week say about the quality of data from questionnaires?

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: I'm pretty sure it recommended questionnaires as a source of 'highly reliable data'. As long as you design the questionnaire properly in the first place, the data will be fine.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: No, I'm sure it talked about drawbacks as well, didn't it? Something about the response rate and the problems you get if it's too low.

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: Yeah, but we only need data from five subjects anyway.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: I suppose so. Another drawback I remember it mentioned was that questionnaire data tends not to reveal anything unexpected, because it is limited to the questions fixed in advance by the researcher.

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: Come on, Rosa. This is only a practice. It's not meant to be real research, is it?

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: Well, I'm not sure about that.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: Maybe I'd better go through the article again, just to be sure. Can you remember what it was called?

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: 'Sample Surveys in Social Science Research'. I think. By Mehta.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: M-E-H-T-A?

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: Yeah. And he also recommended a more recent book, called 'Survey Research', by Bell, I think. It's in that series published by London University.

segments.speaker: PETE
segments.en: And if we tried to use interviews instead, I saw a book in the departmental library

segments.speaker: THAT'LL BE HELPFUL
segments.en: it's called 'Interviews That Work', by Wilson, published in Oxford in nineteen eighty-eight.

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: Right. I've got a tutorial now. Can we meet up again later this week? What about Friday morning?

segments.speaker: PETE
segments.en: Suits me. Eleven o'clock?

segments.speaker: ROSA
segments.en: Fine.

segments.speaker: MICK
segments.en: Before Friday, I think we should all look through the reading list.
